---
title: "Recurrence"
subtitle: "A completed relation can itself become countable"
toc: true
---

Occurrence tells us that something happened.

Closure tells us that a readable state path returned.

Recurrence asks a different question:

> **How many times does the completed relation happen again?**

This distinction is fundamental in R<sup>2</sup>D.

A state can occur many times without completing a closure.

A closure can complete once without recurring.

And completed closures at neighboring boundaries can recur at very different
counts.

R<sup>2</sup>D therefore treats recurrence as its own primitive count
relation.

[Closure →](closure.qmd)

## Occurrence Is Not Recurrence

At boundary $B_n$, the state occurrence count

$$
\nu_{n,i}
$$

counts realized instances classified as macrostate $i$ within a specified
finite realization domain.

Its logarithmic coordinate is

$$
\tau_{n,i}
=
\ln\nu_{n,i}.
$$

This tells us how often realizations associated with a state occur.

But it does not tell us how often an entire closed path completes.

For example, a closure

$$
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}:
i
\rightarrow
k
\rightarrow
i
$$

contains multiple state occurrences.

Counting those individual occurrences is not the same as counting completed
recurrences of

$$
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}.
$$

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{occurrence}
\neq
\text{recurrence}.
}
$$

[Occupancy and Occurrence →](occupancy-occurrence.qmd)

## Closure Creates a Countable Whole

Before closure, we can count individual states and transitions.

After closure, the completed path itself can be treated as one countable
relation.

Schematically:

$$
i
\rightarrow
k
\rightarrow
i
$$

becomes

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
}
$$

as one completed local closure.

If the same closure completes again,

$$
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha},
\quad
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}',
\quad
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}'',
\quad
\dots,
$$

then the closure itself has become recurrent.

This is a crucial step in recursive counting:

> **Completion turns a path into something that can itself be counted.**

## Whole-Closure Recurrence Count

Choose a finite recurrence-comparison domain

$$
\mathcal D_R.
$$

Within that domain, let

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right)
$$

be the number of completed recurrences of local closure

$$
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}.
$$

This is a **whole-closure recurrence count**.

It is not the same as the state occurrence count

$$
\nu_{n,i}.
$$

It is also not the same as the opposed-leg occurrence counts

$$
\nu_{n,\alpha,H}
$$

and

$$
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}.
$$

Those quantities answer different questions.

## Four Counts Must Remain Separate

By this point R<sup>2</sup>D contains several distinct realized counts.

### State occurrence

$$
\nu_{n,i}
$$

asks:

> How many realized instances are classified as state $i$?

### Opposed-leg occurrence

$$
\nu_{n,\alpha,H},
\qquad
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
$$

asks:

> How many times was each complete oriented leg of the closure realized?

### Closure recurrence

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right)
$$

asks:

> How many times did the complete closure recur?

### Enclosing recurrence

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\chi_{n+1}
\right)
$$

asks:

> How many completed realizations of the corresponding enclosing transition
> occurred in the same comparison domain?

These counts must not be collapsed into one quantity.

## Recurrence Does Not Yet Mean Time

The comparison domain

$$
\mathcal D_R
$$

is a domain of count.

It is not assumed to be a physical time interval.

Therefore

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right)
$$

is not yet a frequency.

Likewise, the comparison of recurrence counts across boundaries is not yet a
physical rate.

Part I remains dimensionless.

Physical time appears only later, if a physical system supplies a valid
mapping from recurrence count to temporal measurement.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{recurrence count}
\neq
\text{physical time}.
}
$$

## Adjacent Boundaries Can Recur Differently

Now consider a local closure at $B_n$,

$$
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha},
$$

and its corresponding enclosing transition class at $B_{n+1}$,

$$
\chi_{n+1}.
$$

Count both within the same recurrence-comparison domain

$$
\mathcal D_R.
$$

Let

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right)
$$

be the number of completed local closure recurrences,

and

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\chi_{n+1}
\right)
$$

the number of completed enclosing recurrences.

R<sup>2</sup>D then defines their relative recurrence.

## The Adjacent Recurrence Ratio

For

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right)>0,
$$

define

$$
\boxed{
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}
=
\frac{
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\chi_{n+1}
\right)
}{
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right)
}.
}
$$

The ratio asks:

> **How many enclosing recurrences are realized per completed recurrence of
> the representative local closure?**

This is one of the central across-boundary count relations in
R<sup>2</sup>D.

## A Simple Example

Suppose within one recurrence-comparison domain a local closure completes

$$
1000
$$

times.

Suppose the corresponding enclosing transition completes

$$
10
$$

times.

Then

$$
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}
=
\frac{10}{1000}
=
0.01.
$$

The enclosing relation recurs once for every one hundred recurrences of the
local closure.

Nothing in this example requires seconds, hertz, or a physical clock.

It is purely a ratio of completed counts.

## The Ratio Is Independent of Comparison-Domain Size

Suppose the same stationary recurrence relation persists while the comparison
domain is enlarged.

If

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right)
$$

and

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\chi_{n+1}
\right)
$$

scale proportionally, then their ratio remains unchanged.

For example,

$$
\frac{10}{1000}
=
\frac{100}{10000}.
$$

Thus

$$
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}
$$

describes the relative recurrence structure rather than the arbitrary size of
the domain over which it was counted.

## Logarithmic Recurrence Scaling

As elsewhere in R<sup>2</sup>D, a multiplicative ratio can be represented
logarithmically.

For

$$
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}>0,
$$

define

$$
\boxed{
\gamma_{n+1|n,\alpha}
=
\ln
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}.
}
$$

This is the logarithmic recurrence scaling between adjacent boundaries.

Again,

$$
\gamma
$$

is dimensionless.

It is not yet elapsed time, frequency, or rate.

## A Zero Recurrence Ratio Is Allowed

Suppose the local closure recurs,

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right)>0,
$$

but the corresponding enclosing transition does not recur within the
comparison domain:

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\chi_{n+1}
\right)=0.
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}=0.
}
$$

This is permitted.

It means:

> **The local closure can recur while the enclosing relation has not yet
> completed a recurrence within the same count domain.**

This distinction becomes extremely important at large recursive boundaries.

A smaller-scale process may appear repeatedly active while a larger enclosing
relation appears effectively motionless.

## Recurrence Is Different From Reciprocal Realization

Recall the closure efficiency

$$
\eta_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\frac{
\nu_{n,\alpha,L}
}{
\nu_{n,\alpha,H}
}.
$$

This asks whether the two opposed closure legs are realized with equal
occurrence-count efficiency.

The recurrence ratio

$$
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}
$$

asks something completely different.

It compares the number of completed recurrences across adjacent boundaries.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\eta
\neq
\rho.
}
$$

A closure can have reciprocal opposed-leg realization

$$
\eta=1
$$

while recurring at a very different count from its enclosing transition.

Likewise, nonreciprocal occurrence realization does not itself tell us how
often the whole closure recurs.

## Recurrence Is Different From Closure Asymmetry

Closure asymmetry is

$$
\Delta A_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
=
\Delta P_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
-
\Delta R_{n,\alpha,\mathcal C}.
$$

This measures the directional relation remaining around a completed closure.

Recurrence asks how often that completed closure itself repeats.

Therefore:

$$
\boxed{
\Delta A_{\mathcal C}
\neq
\rho.
}
$$

One describes direction.

The other describes relative recurrence.

The distinction between the two becomes essential in the R<sup>2</sup>D law.

## Recurrence Is Different From Recursive Carry

Recursive carry asks how a completed local realization is reclassified when
the boundary changes:

$$
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}.
$$

The recurrence ratio asks how often the two boundary-specific realizations
recur relative to one another.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{carry}
\neq
\text{recurrence}.
}
$$

Carry is a classification relation.

Recurrence is a count relation.

[Recursive Carry →](recursive-carry.qmd)

## One Recursive Relation, Different Recurrence Counts

A local closure and an enclosing occurrence can be two boundary-specific
readings of one recursively organized relation.

But this does not require a one-to-one correspondence between their
recurrence counts.

In general,

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right)
\neq
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\chi_{n+1}
\right).
$$

This is why R<sup>2</sup>D needs

$$
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}.
$$

The ratio preserves the recursive relation without requiring identical count
rates at adjacent boundaries.

## Recurrence Creates Scale

This suggests a primitive meaning of scale.

Two boundaries can be recursively related while their completed relations
recur at very different counts.

A subordinate boundary may complete many recurrences during one recurrence
of its enclosing boundary.

Schematically:

$$
\underbrace{
\mathcal C_n
\mathcal C_n
\mathcal C_n
\mathcal C_n
\mathcal C_n
}_{\text{many local recurrences}}
\quad
\longleftrightarrow
\quad
\underbrace{
\chi_{n+1}
}_{\text{one enclosing recurrence}}.
$$

The distinction between "fast" and "slow" can therefore begin as a count
relation before physical time is assigned.

That is the basis of the recursive clock developed later in the Canon.

## The Recursive Clock

Imagine recursively nested closures.

A small boundary closes repeatedly.

Its enclosing boundary closes less often.

A still larger boundary may require many lower-boundary recurrences before
one enclosing recurrence is completed.

The hierarchy can be pictured as nested gears:

$$
B_n
\rightarrow
B_{n+1}
\rightarrow
B_{n+2}
\rightarrow
\cdots
$$

with each boundary carrying its own completed recurrence.

The gear metaphor is useful only if the causal architecture is kept clear.

The smaller gear does not independently generate the larger one.

Rather, the recursively organized relation has different readable recurrence
counts at different boundaries.

> **Recurrence provides the primitive ordering from which physical clock
> readings can later emerge.**

## A Large Boundary Can Appear Motionless

Suppose

$$
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}
\ll1.
$$

Then many local closures occur for each enclosing recurrence.

To an observer restricted to the local count domain, the enclosing relation
may appear nearly fixed.

Yet it can still organize the local realization.

This gives R<sup>2</sup>D a useful distinction:

$$
\boxed{
\text{slow enclosing recurrence}
\neq
\text{absence of enclosing organization}.
}
$$

A boundary does not have to visibly complete a cycle during the observation
domain in order to define compatibility for subordinate realization.

## Recurrence Before Physical Rate

Later physical science may supply a mapping such as

$$
\text{recurrence count}
\longrightarrow
\text{frequency}
$$

or

$$
\text{recurrence ratio}
\longrightarrow
\text{relative physical rate}.
$$

But the logical order matters.

R<sup>2</sup>D begins with

$$
\boxed{
\text{completed recurrence counts}
}
$$

and only afterward asks whether a physical clock or frequency coordinate
reads them.

This reverses the assumption that time must already exist before recurrence
can be counted.

## A Clock Is a Physical Read of Recurrence

A physical clock works by recurrence.

A pendulum repeats.

A quartz crystal oscillates.

An atomic transition recurs.

A rotating object cycles.

In conventional physics, these recurrences are used to measure an already
assumed temporal coordinate.

R<sup>2</sup>D asks whether the logical direction can be reversed:

$$
\boxed{
\text{recurrence}
\rightarrow
\text{physical clock read}.
}
$$

Part I does not yet claim a specific physical clock mapping.

It establishes only the primitive count relation that such a mapping would
have to read.

## Recurrence and Distinguishability Form Complementary Coordinates

A closure contains at least two primitive aspects.

There is **what distinction is traversed**:

$$
\lambda_n.
$$

And there is **how that completed distinction recurs relative to another
boundary**:

$$
\rho_{n+1|n}.
$$

These are different count relations.

One describes distinguishable interval.

The other describes recursive repetition.

Later parts of R<sup>2</sup>D ask what happens when both remain readable, or
when one becomes unreadable while the other remains accessible.

This becomes the basis of the later readability horizons.

## Across More Than One Boundary

Suppose we have a recursive chain

$$
B_n
\rightarrow
B_{n+1}
\rightarrow
B_{n+2}.
$$

Define adjacent recurrence ratios

$$
\rho_{n+1|n}
$$

and

$$
\rho_{n+2|n+1}.
$$

Because they are ratios, their recursive composition is multiplicative:

$$
\boxed{
\rho_{n+2|n}
=
\rho_{n+2|n+1}
\rho_{n+1|n}.
}
$$

Taking logarithms gives additive recurrence scaling:

$$
\boxed{
\gamma_{n+2|n}
=
\gamma_{n+2|n+1}
+
\gamma_{n+1|n}.
}
$$

The same architecture extends through a hierarchy of boundaries.

This is the next step: **recursive counting across scale**.

[Recursive Counting Across Scale →](recursive-counting.qmd)

## Why Recurrence Matters for the R<sup>2</sup>D Law

The local closure and enclosing occurrence are related recursively.

But they need not recur one-for-one.

The R<sup>2</sup>D law therefore cannot compare local and enclosing
distinguishability alone.

It must also account for their relative recurrence.

That is why the recurrence ratio

$$
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}
$$

enters the bridge between local closure geometry and enclosing constrained
geometry.

Direction alone is not enough.

Distinguishability alone is not enough.

The recursive relation also has a recurrence structure.

[The R²D Law →](r2d-law.qmd)

## The Architecture So Far

The primitive hierarchy can now be written:

$$
\boxed{
\text{distinction}
\rightarrow
\text{change}
\rightarrow
\text{return}
\rightarrow
\text{closure}
\rightarrow
\text{recurrence}
\rightarrow
\text{recursive comparison}.
}
$$

Each step adds a new count relation.

A distinction can change.

A changed state can return.

A return can belong to an enclosing occurrence and become closure.

A closure can recur.

And recurrence at one boundary can be compared with recurrence at another.

This is why recurrence is not merely repetition.

It is the bridge that makes recursive counting possible.

---

## Core Equations

### Whole-closure recurrence count

$$
\boxed{
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right)
}
$$

### Enclosing recurrence count

$$
\boxed{
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\chi_{n+1}
\right)
}
$$

### Adjacent recurrence ratio

$$
\boxed{
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}
=
\frac{
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\chi_{n+1}
\right)
}{
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right)
}
}
$$

### Logarithmic recurrence scaling

$$
\boxed{
\gamma_{n+1|n,\alpha}
=
\ln
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}
}
$$

### Recursive composition

$$
\boxed{
\rho_{N|n}
=
\prod_{j=n}^{N-1}
\rho_{j+1|j}
}
$$

and therefore

$$
\boxed{
\ln\rho_{N|n}
=
\sum_{j=n}^{N-1}
\ln\rho_{j+1|j}.
}
$$

---

## The Key Distinction

The simplest summary is:

> **Occurrence counts realized states.**

> **Closure identifies a completed local return compatible with an enclosing
> occurrence.**

> **Recurrence counts repeated completion of that closure.**

> **The recurrence ratio compares completed recurrence across boundaries.**

None of these quantities requires physical time.

Time can come later as a physical read of recurrence.

The next step is to ask what happens when recurrence ratios compose through
many recursively nested boundaries.
